titulo.texto: Hall Five: Tláloc, the Blue Pot, and Offering Forty-One

frase_gancho.texto: A blue pot, a numbered offering, and the helpers of the rain.

puente_narrativo.texto: When you are ready, continue to the next stop on your tour.

guion_corto.texto: Hall five corresponds to the north side of the temple, the side of Tláloc. It brings together a pot painted blue, offering forty-one, and representations of the tlaloque, the helpers of the rain. This side of the temple was associated with water and fertility, and it complemented the south side, the side of war. The hall invites you to think about what rain meant for a city on a lake, and why the Mexica placed it at the center of their main temple. It is a calmer hall than the previous one, and it is best explored without hurry, looking at each display case separately.

guion_largo.texto:
You now cross over to the other side of the temple. Hall five is dedicated to Tláloc, the god of rain, and to what was found in the shrine on the north side.

Remember what you saw in the archaeological zone, at the stop for the two shrines. The pyramid had two shrines: to the south, Huitzilopochtli, and to the north, Tláloc. Each one was a sacred mountain, and each one called for different offerings. This hall is the mirror of the previous one: instead of war and the Sun, the theme is water, fertility, and sustenance.

One of the main objects is a pot painted blue. It is a ceremonial piece. The color blue is often associated with water, and it is one of the features that help identify this god. As you enter the hall, notice how that color changes the atmosphere compared with the previous one.

The hall also displays offering forty-one. Archaeologists number the offerings of the Templo Mayor, and this is one of those found on the side of Tláloc. More than one hundred offerings have been found in total, as you saw in hall one. Each one has its own number and its own list of objects, and that is why they can be studied one by one. This order is part of the archaeologists’ work, as they record where each thing was before moving it.

There are also representations of the tlaloque. According to tradition, they were the helpers of Tláloc, in charge of the rain. They were imagined as small beings who poured water from vessels. In the hall you can look for their figures and notice how they were depicted. The signs in the hall will tell you more about each one, and they are worth reading calmly.

Think about why Tláloc was at the center of the city. Tenochtitlan stood on an island, surrounded by lakes, and depended on the rain and on water levels. A drought or a flood could be catastrophic. Having the god of rain in the main temple was a way of acknowledging that dependence.

A tip for looking more closely: compare this hall with the previous one. There you saw an Eagle Warrior, a fire serpent, and figures of gods of fire and death. Here the focus turns to water and to the earth that bears fruit. Together, the two halls tell the story of the temple’s duality.

Before you leave, return for a moment to the blue pot and compare it with what you saw on the side of Huitzilopochtli. That comparison helps you see both sides of the temple. As you leave, continue to the next stop on your tour.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Tláloc was a minor god at the Templo Mayor.
texto.respuesta: Reality: He shared the top of the pyramid with Huitzilopochtli; each one had his own shrine.
